topic: Speed beats polish when winning clients
caption:
Nobody hires the agency with the best deck.

I have lost pitches with better slides.
I have won pitches with no slides at all.

The difference was nearly always the same thing.
Who picked up the phone first.

A business owner with a burst pipe, a lawsuit or a dead website does not compare decks.
They call three people.
They hire the one who answers.

So we answer in minutes, not days.
It has won us more clients than any proposal.

#SmallBusiness #Marketing

topic: Speed beats polish when winning clients
caption:
Most ad accounts do not need more budget.

They need fewer keywords.

The pattern I see every week:
Results drop, so the owner raises the budget.
The extra money goes to the same broad terms that were already failing.
Cost per lead goes up, not down.

What works is the opposite.
Cut the account back to the 20 terms that bring in buyers.
Block everything else.
Then add budget.

Less coverage. More customers.

#GoogleAds #PPC

topic: Speed to lead, Harvard Business Review
caption:
23% of US firms never replied to a web enquiry at all.

Harvard Business Review sent enquiries to 2,241 companies.
37% replied within an hour.
16% took 1 to 24 hours.
24% took longer than a day.
23% never answered.

Most businesses think they have a lead problem.
A lot of them have a reply problem.

Before you spend another dollar on ads, test it yourself.
Fill in your own contact form and time how long the reply takes.

Source: HBR, "The Short Life of Online Sales Leads", 2011.

The fastest fix in paid ads is often not in the ads.

topic: Google reviews as a filter: buyers drop a business on star rating, review count and how old the newest review is (BrightLocal 2026)
caption:
47% of US buyers will not use a business with fewer than 20 reviews.

That comes from BrightLocal's 2026 survey of 1,002 adults.
So a plumber with 12 reviews loses close to half of the buyers who look him up.

The same survey has four more numbers every owner should know.
97% read reviews for local businesses.
89% expect the owner to reply.
74% look for reviews from the last three months.
68% will only use a business rated 4 stars or more.

That last figure was 55% a year earlier.
The bar went up in twelve months, and nobody sent owners a memo.

Take an example profile with 14 reviews, the newest from June, and no replies.
Every buyer sees that before they ever see his prices.
The owner is paying to be filtered out.

The fix is boring and it works on any budget.
Ask every customer after every job, reply to every review, and reach 20 before you raise the ad spend.

How many reviews does your profile have today?

Source: BrightLocal, Local Consumer Review Survey, 2026.

topic: Websites that act like brochures instead of salespeople (Farhan) and conversion tracking that counts page views as conversions (Nasir)
caption:
A brochure tells people you exist.
A salesperson gets them to call.

Most local service websites I open are still brochures.
A nice truck photo, the word "quality" in every heading, and the phone number hidden in the footer.

A website that sells does three jobs on the first screen.
It says what you do and which towns you cover.
It shows proof, like reviews and photos of real jobs.
It gives one next step, a call button or a short form.

The words matter more than the design.
Unbounce studied more than 41,000 landing pages for its 2024 benchmark.
The median page converted 6.6% of visitors.
Pages written at a 5th to 7th grade reading level converted at 11.1%, against 5.3% for professional-level writing.

Plain words roughly doubled the rate in that data.

So read your homepage out loud to someone who has never heard of you.
If they cannot tell you what you do and how to book within 10 seconds, it is still a brochure.

Which line on your homepage would a customer skip first?

Source: Unbounce, Conversion Benchmark Report, 2024.

topic: Google reviews as a filter: buyers drop a business on star rating, review count and how old the newest review is (BrightLocal 2026)
caption:
74% of US buyers look for reviews written in the last three months.

A 4.8 rating with nothing new since August can read like a business that stopped picking up.

I check the date on the newest review before I touch an ad budget.
Paid clicks, map results and AI answers land on that same Google profile.
When it looks stale, every click I pay for starts with a doubt.

BrightLocal's 2026 recency figures moved fast in a year.
32% want a review from the past two weeks, up from 20%.
18% are only swayed by reviews from the past week.
19% expect the owner to reply the same day, up from 6%.

December makes all of this worse.
Jobs slow down, nobody asks for reviews, and by late January the newest one is two months old.

The floor I use is one new review a week.
That keeps a fresh one inside the two-week window almost all the time.
Ask every customer, and plan on about half of them writing one.

When was the newest review on your profile posted?

Source: BrightLocal, Local Consumer Review Survey, 2026.

topic: Chasing one huge keyword: an owner who wants to rank nationwide for "plumber" (Farhan) and broad match keywords on a $20 a day budget (Nasir)
caption:
A plumber who serves one county gains nothing from ranking nationwide for "plumber".

He needs to show up in the map for the towns his vans can reach.

The request sounds ambitious, so it is easy to say yes to.
It is the wrong target.

Google says local results are based mainly on relevance, distance and prominence.
Distance means a homeowner in Ohio will never see a Texas plumber in the map, however good his website is.

Whitespark tested 540 local searches in 2025.
On searches with clear local intent, a local pack showed up 93% of the time.
"Plumber" is about as local as a search gets.

So the better question is about money.
Which jobs pay best, in which towns, and what do people type when they need them?

That gives you a list like "water heater repair Plano" or "emergency plumber Frisco".
Each one has fewer searches.
Every one of them comes from someone close enough to hire you.

A national ranking for one huge word is a trophy.
A page for each service and town, plus a strong Google profile, is a business.

What is the one search you would most like to win in your own town?

Sources: Google Business Profile Help, 2026. Whitespark, 2025.

#LocalSEO #SEO

topic: Websites that act like brochures instead of salespeople (Farhan) and conversion tracking that counts page views as conversions (Nasir)
caption:
If a page view counts as a conversion, Google Ads will go and buy you more page views.

It is one of the first things I check in a new account.
A "thank you page" goal gets set up, the page also loads for people who never sent the form, and the Conversions column fills up.

Smart Bidding then does exactly what it was told.
It finds cheap visitors who load pages, and it gets very good at finding them.

Google's help page spells out the rule.
Primary actions are "reported in the 'Conversions' column in your reports and used for bidding".
Secondary actions are kept for reporting only.

The check takes about 15 minutes:
1. Open Goals, then Conversions, then Summary, and list every primary action.
2. Keep calls, submitted forms and qualified leads as primary.
3. Move page views, button clicks and directions to secondary.
4. Count leads as "One" per click, as Google suggests for leads.

Expect the column to drop afterwards.
Google says bidding may need 1 to 2 conversion cycles to adapt to new goals.
The number gets smaller and starts telling the truth.

Which actions are set to primary in your account right now?

Source: Google Ads Help, primary and secondary conversion actions, 2026.

#GoogleAds
alt: A dark tweet-style card from Nasir Ahmad saying that if a page view is set as a primary conversion, Google is buying you page views.

topic: Cheap marketing ends up the most expensive (Farhan) and if you cannot track the call you cannot fix the ad (Nasir)
caption:
Cheap marketing is the most expensive thing a small business buys, because you pay for it twice.

Once for the work.
Then again to undo it.

The cheap offers look alike.
An SEO package that promises page one, fast.
Links from sites nobody has ever read.
A batch of five-star reviews from strangers.

Google's own guide to hiring an SEO says no one can guarantee a number one ranking on Google.
Anyone who guarantees it is promising something Google itself will not.

The reviews are worse.
The FTC's final rule from August 2024 bans fake and bought reviews, and it can seek civil penalties.
Google goes further and bans paying for reviews even when the reward does not depend on a good one.

The cleanup is where the real cost sits.
Bad links, a suspended Google profile or a site rebuilt around the wrong pages can take months to undo.
Those months have no leads in them.

So before you sign anything cheap, ask the seller one thing.
What exactly will you do each month, and how will I see it?
If the answer is vague, the price was never the cheap part.

What is the most expensive cheap thing you have bought for your business?

Sources: Google Search Central, 2026. FTC, 2024.

#SEO #SmallBusiness
alt: Quote card from Mohd Farhan reading: Cheap marketing is the most expensive thing you will buy. The bill just arrives later.

topic: Chasing one huge keyword: an owner who wants to rank nationwide for "plumber" (Farhan) and broad match keywords on a $20 a day budget (Nasir)
caption:
$20 a day on broad match mostly buys Google's guesses about your customers.

On a budget that size, there is too little data for those guesses to get good.

The arithmetic, with LocaliQ's 2026 averages of $5.42 a click and an 8.18% conversion rate:
$20 a day is about $600 a month.
$600 buys about 110 clicks.
110 clicks bring about 9 conversions.

Google recommends judging Smart Bidding over periods with at least 30 conversions.
It also says "it's critical to use Smart Bidding with broad match".
So at $20 a day, broad match is learning from about 9 data points a month.

Meanwhile it matches your keyword to searches "related" to it.
In a plumbing account, that can mean salaries, trade schools and DIY videos.

The independent data points the same way.
Optmyzr's study of 992,028 keywords found a 415% return on ad spend for exact match and 277% for broad.

What I run on budgets this size:
Exact and phrase match on the few terms that bring real jobs.
A negative list, built from the search terms report every week.
Broad match only once the account tracks about 30 real conversions a month.

What does your search terms report show for last week?

Sources: LocaliQ, 2026. Optmyzr, 2024. Google Ads Help, 2026.

#GoogleAds #PPC

topic: The 3 stages of the monthly agency report (Farhan) and the 3 stages of the Meta learning phase (Nasir)
caption:
A monthly report with no calls and no booked jobs in it was written for the agency.

Impressions, clicks, average position and a chart that goes up.
All of them are real numbers.
None of them pays the rent.

This is not only an agency habit.
In Litmus's 2025 State of Email survey, 21% of marketing leaders said they do not measure email return at all.
If marketers skip the money number, owners get reports that skip it too.

A useful report for a local business starts with four lines:
1. Calls and forms this month, split by source.
2. Booked jobs or sales from them, if you track it.
3. Spend, and the cost of each real lead.
4. What changed this month, and what changes next month.

Everything else can sit below those four lines.
If you have to scroll past ten pages of charts to find the calls, ask why.

A good agency can explain a bad month in one paragraph.
A weak one sends you more pages.

What is the first number you look for when the report lands?

Source: Litmus, State of Email, 2025.

#SmallBusiness #Marketing

topic: Cheap marketing ends up the most expensive (Farhan) and if you cannot track the call you cannot fix the ad (Nasir)
caption:
If a lead business cannot see which ad made the phone ring, every change to that account is a guess.

Most local trades sell by phone.
Many ad accounts still count web forms only.

That does damage in two places.
The cost per lead looks far higher than it really is, so good campaigns get paused.
And Smart Bidding never learns which searches end in a call, so it cannot find more of them.

The fix costs less than most owners expect.
Google Ads can swap the number on your site for a Google forwarding number, which Google says is "without any cost to you".
That covers people who clicked an ad.

To track every source, including the map listing and Facebook, you need a paid tool.
Published entry prices are $30 a month for WhatConverts, $50 for CallRail and $79 for CTM, plus usage.

Then listen to a few calls each week.
Invoca's 2026 home services data found only 52% of inbound calls reached a person.
Sometimes the ad is fine and the leak is the phone.

Do you know which campaign your last 10 calls came from?

Sources: Google Ads Help, 2026. Vendor pricing pages, 2026. Invoca, 2026.

#GoogleAds #PPC

topic: December leads: urgent jobs keep coming in during the slow weeks, so keep the phone and the account ready (Google Trends 2025 to 2026)
caption:
December is quieter for most local trades, but the calls that still come in are the urgent ones.

Google Trends shows the split.
In December 2025, US searches for "plumber" ran at 64% of their peak month, and "electrician" at 66%.
"Lawn care" fell to 35%.

Things that break keep ringing.
Things people plan wait for spring.

That changes what an owner should do this month.
Keep the phone answered, including the week between Christmas and New Year.
Set holiday hours on your Google profile, even for days you open as normal, which Google suggests.
Move ad money toward emergency jobs instead of switching everything off.

Then use the quiet weeks for the spring work.
Lawn care searches more than doubled from December to March in the same data.
Pages and ads for spring jobs written now are live when those searches arrive.

The video shows an example week, not a real client.
The pattern in it is the one the search data describes.

What does your phone look like in the last two weeks of December?

Source: Google Trends, US, November 2025 to August 2026.

#LocalSEO #SmallBusiness

topic: The 3 stages of the monthly agency report (Farhan) and the 3 stages of the Meta learning phase (Nasir)
caption:
Most small Meta budgets never get out of the learning phase, and the arithmetic shows why.

Meta says an ad set usually leaves learning after about 50 results in the week after its last significant edit.
A result is the event you optimize for, so that means 50 leads, not 50 clicks.

WordStream's 2025 benchmarks put the average home services lead at $41.26.
Fifty of those is about $2,063 a week, in a single ad set.
That is close to $300 a day before the ad set has even settled.

Meta is open about what learning costs.
It says ad sets in learning are "less stable and usually have a higher CPA".

What I do on small budgets:
Fewer ad sets, so the results pool in one place.
No edits for a week once something starts working.
No pauses of 7 days or more, because Meta counts that as a significant edit too.

And when the column says Learning limited, I read it as a budget message.
Meta says it is not a penalty.
It means the setup cannot reach about 50 results a week.

How many ad sets is your Meta budget split across right now?

Sources: Meta Business Help Center, 2026. WordStream, 2025.

#MetaAds

topic: Found photos that show behaviour: one checkout lane open with a long queue (Farhan, one phone line for all leads) and footprints in snow ignoring the paved path (Nasir, the search terms report)
caption:
One open checkout and a queue to the back of the store is what a single phone line does to your leads.

The people at the front get served.
The ones at the back put the basket down and walk out.

Phones behave the same way, and there is data on it.
Invoca's 2026 home services benchmarks found 52% of inbound calls reached a person.
In CallRail's 2025 survey of 1,000 US consumers, 21% said they call another business straight away when nobody answers.

For the owner of a 3-van HVAC company, that is the Monday after a cold snap.
You are on one call, the office line rings out, and the job goes to the next name on the map.

More ads will not fix this.
They only make the queue longer.

Opening a second lane is cheaper than most owners expect:
Calls that ring two phones at once, or roll to a second person after four rings.
An answering service for evenings and weekends.
A text back within minutes for every missed call.

This is a good week to set it up, before the holiday run of burst pipes and no-heat calls.

How many people can answer your business phone right now?

Sources: Invoca, 2026. CallRail, 2025.

topic: December leads: urgent jobs keep coming in during the slow weeks, so keep the phone and the account ready (Google Trends 2025 to 2026)
caption:
In late January 2026, US searches for "snow removal" jumped about elevenfold in a single week.

That was the week a winter storm brought ice warnings from East Texas to the Carolinas.
"Frozen pipes" went from under 1 on the Google Trends scale to 17 in the same week.
"Plumber" rose from between 57 and 63 to 72.

That is why I do not plan winter accounts month by month.
Demand comes in spikes, and the account has to be ready before the storm arrives.

My list for the last days of December:
Holiday hours set on the Google profile.
Ad schedule matched to the hours someone answers the phone.
Emergency terms like "frozen pipe" and "no heat" kept live, with budget room to spare.
Spring campaigns drafted now, so they launch on time.

The stakes on those calls are high.
State Farm says its average frozen pipe claim was over $30,000.

Shops have a different December.
In a Google and Ipsos survey, shoppers did about 24% of their holiday shopping in the two weeks before Christmas 2024.
For a store, this week is a quarter of the season.

Which search would bring you the most calls if a storm hit tomorrow?

Sources: Google Trends, 2026. Google and Ipsos, 2024. State Farm, 2025.

#GoogleAds #LocalSEO

An account only holds a return like this for seven years if someone keeps catching that drift, week after week.
The checks that catch it are dull, and they have to run every single week.

If you are setting next year's ad budget this week, judge your account over years, not over one December.

topic: Found photos that show behaviour: one checkout lane open with a long queue (Farhan, one phone line for all leads) and footprints in snow ignoring the paved path (Nasir, the search terms report)
caption:
Fresh snow shows where people really walk, and it is rarely the path somebody paved for them.

Ad accounts have their own snow.
It is called the search terms report.

You choose keywords.
Customers type whatever they like.
Google decides which of those searches count as a match.
Broad match is now the default for every keyword, according to Google, so it decides a lot.

The report is where the real route shows up.
You see the searches that turned into calls, and the ones that spent money and never came close.

Every Monday I sort it into three piles.
Searches to add as keywords of their own, because buyers use those exact words.
Searches to block as negatives.
Searches to leave for another week, because there is not enough data yet.

The second pile is where the savings are.
The first pile is where growth usually hides.

It is Christmas Eve, so your report can wait until Monday.
Just do not let it wait until February.

What is the strangest search term you have found in your own account?

Source: Google Ads Help, keyword matching options, 2026.

topic: End of year: big January marketing plans that stall by week three (Farhan) and pausing ads over Christmas that sends the account back into learning (Nasir)
caption:
Most January marketing plans stall by week three, because they have no owner and no time slot.

New website, start SEO, run ads, post every day.
Then the business gets busy again and the plan sits in a notes app.

For local trades the calendar adds pressure.
In Google Trends, US searches for lawn care more than doubled from December to March.
Seasonal work needs the plan live by the time the phones get busy.

The plans I see survive have three things:
One person who owns it, by name.
One weekly slot in the calendar, with a day and an hour.
One number to check every Friday, like calls from the website.

Everything else is a wish list.

So before you write the 2027 plan, cut it down.
Pick the one job that would bring the most calls in the first 90 days.
If people cannot find you, that is the Google profile and reviews.
If they find you and do not call, that is the website.

Then put the first hour of work in the calendar for the first week of January.

Which one job is going into your calendar first?

Source: Google Trends, US, December 2025 to March 2026.

#SmallBusiness #Marketing

What I watch every week on an account like this:
Search terms, for new junk to block.
Cost per conversion by campaign, because a good total can hide one bad campaign.
Conversion tracking, which breaks more often than people think after a site change.

If you are looking back over 2026 this week, check your weakest two weeks as closely as your best two.

topic: Email benchmarks: click rates by industry and the self-reported $36 ROI (Farhan), automated flows earning about 3.3 times the clicks of one-off campaigns (Nasir)
caption:
Construction businesses had a 3.53% median email click rate in 2025, over three times the 1.07% for online stores.

Those are MailerLite's medians from 3.6 million campaigns sent between December 2024 and November 2025.
Legal led the list at 4.90%.
Beauty and personal care came last at 0.95%.

The pattern is easy to read.
Businesses that send fewer, more useful emails earn more clicks than ones that send an offer every few days.

The return side is harder to pin down.
The famous $36 back for every $1 comes from Litmus surveys of marketers, and it is self-reported.
In Litmus's 2025 survey, 21% of marketing leaders said they do not measure email return at all.

So for 2027, measure two things on every send.
Clicks, against your own industry's median.
Calls, bookings or sales in the week after it goes out.

At the 2.09% median across all industries, a roofer with 2,000 past customers gets about 42 clicks per email.
That is 42 past customers thinking about the roof again.

What was the click rate on your last email?

Sources: MailerLite, 2025. Litmus, State of Email, 2025.

#EmailMarketing #SmallBusiness

topic: End of year: big January marketing plans that stall by week three (Farhan) and pausing ads over Christmas that sends the account back into learning (Nasir)
caption:
Pausing ads for Christmas often costs more in January than it saved in December.

Both Google and Meta make the account relearn when you switch it back on.

Google says a bid strategy that was recently created or reactivated shows a Learning status for up to 7 days.
Meta counts pausing an ad set for 7 days or longer as a significant edit, which sends it back into learning.
And during learning, Meta says, ad sets are less stable and usually cost more per result.

So the first week of January, when people come back looking for quotes, runs on an account that is relearning.

What I do over the holidays instead:
Lower the budget rather than switching campaigns off.
Set the ad schedule to the hours someone answers the phone.
Keep emergency and high-intent terms running.
Leave bids and targeting alone until the second week of January.

Budget changes are the safe lever in Google.
Google says they never remove your historical data, and they do not trigger Learning.

If you already paused, nothing is broken.
Switch it back on before the weekend, and expect a slower first week.

Did you pause your ads this year, or keep them running?

Sources: Google Ads Help, 2026. Meta Business Help Center, 2026.

#GoogleAds #MetaAds

topic: Email benchmarks: click rates by industry and the self-reported $36 ROI (Farhan), automated flows earning about 3.3 times the clicks of one-off campaigns (Nasir)
caption:
Automated email flows averaged a 5.58% click rate on Klaviyo, against 1.69% for one-off campaigns.

That is about 3.3 times the clicks, from emails you only build once.
A flow is an email that sends itself when someone does something, like signing up or leaving a cart.

Plenty of small accounts have this the wrong way round.
A newsletter every week, written by hand.
No welcome email and no cart reminder running underneath it.

The ceiling is higher too.
Klaviyo's top 10% of flows reached a 10.48% click rate.

Judge flows on clicks, and ignore the open rate.
Litmus counted Apple at 76.56% of recorded opens in September 2026.
Apple Mail Privacy Protection can log an open that no person made.

If you set up one email job this January, make it the welcome flow.
A thank you, one piece of proof, and one clear next step.
Then leave it running and check its click rate once a month.

Which flow is running in your account today?

Sources: Klaviyo email benchmarks, checked 2026. Litmus, 2026.

#EmailMarketing
alt: Dark stat card showing automated email flows get 3.3 times the clicks of one-off campaigns on Klaviyo, with tiles for a 5.58% flow click rate and a 1.69% campaign click rate.

topic: New year goal for 2027: fewer channels done properly / fix tracking before anything else
caption:
My one marketing goal for every client in 2027 is fewer channels, done properly.

In January most owners want to be everywhere.
Google Ads, Facebook, TikTok, SEO, a newsletter, maybe a podcast.

On a $1,000 a month budget, that plan fails on the math.

LocaliQ's 2026 benchmarks put the average search ad lead at $66.69.
So $1,000 buys about 15 leads a month.
Google says to judge Smart Bidding over a period with at least 30 conversions.

One channel at $1,000 is already short of what Google wants to learn from.
Split the same money five ways and each channel gets $200 and almost no data.

So my advice to new clients this year is to pick two.
For a local trade that is usually Google search ads and the Google Business Profile.
Run those well for 90 days, then add a third once the first two pay for it.

If you had to drop all but two channels on Monday, which two would you keep?

Source: LocaliQ search advertising benchmarks, 2026. Google Ads Help.

#SmallBusiness #Marketing
alt: Quote card from Mohd Farhan: One goal for 2027, fewer channels done properly. Five channels done badly lose to two done well.

topic: New year goal for 2027: fewer channels done properly / fix tracking before anything else
caption:
The first thing I open in any account this January is the conversion list, not the ads.

Google bids toward whatever you mark as a primary conversion.
Its own help page says those are the actions used for bidding.

So if a page view is set as primary, the system goes looking for more people who view pages.
For a roofer paying for every click, that is a cheap conversion that never pays an invoice.

Three faults I look for before anything else:
A page view or button click counted as a lead.
Calls from ads not counted at all, because call reporting was never switched on.
A call length set below Google's 60 second default, so misdials count as leads.

Each one teaches the bidding to buy the wrong people.
And every report built on top of that data is wrong too.

Fix those three first.
Then raise the budget, test new ads or change bids, in that order.

What does your Google Ads account count as a conversion right now?

Source: Google Ads Help, primary conversions and call reporting.

#GoogleAds #PPC
alt: Quote card from Nasir Ahmad: Fix the tracking before you touch the budget. Bad data makes smart bidding dumb.

topic: AI Overviews take clicks from question pages, not hire-me searches / why ChatGPT names a competitor
caption:
Your blog traffic can fall this year while your calls stay exactly where they were.

That is what AI Overviews are doing to most local businesses.

Pew Research Center tracked 900 US adults on Google in March 2025.
With an AI summary on the page, they clicked a normal result on 8% of visits.
Without one, 15%.

Now look at which searches get the summary.
Whitespark checked 540 local searches in Houston, Phoenix and Denver.
Questions like "how long does an eye exam take" got an AI Overview 92% of the time.
Searches to hire someone, like "plumber Phoenix", got one 15% of the time and a map pack 93% of the time.

So the clicks you lose come mostly from people reading, not people hiring.

If you own a roofing company, judge your blog by the enquiries it brings in.
Put the real effort into the Google Business Profile, where the map still wins.

When did you last count how many calls your blog brought in?

Source: Pew Research Center, 2025. Whitespark, 2025.

#SEO #LocalSEO

topic: AI Overviews take clicks from question pages, not hire-me searches / why ChatGPT names a competitor
caption:
If ChatGPT names your competitor and not you, the reason is usually on other people's websites.

Whitespark looked at where AI answers got their facts for plumber searches.
60% of the citations went to third-party sites.
40% went to the plumbers' own sites.

So the AI is reading directories, local news, trade groups and review sites about you.
If your rival is mentioned on those pages and you are missing, the rival gets named.

What I check when an owner asks me this:
The business name, address and phone match on every listing.
Reviews are recent and every one has a reply.
The business is named on the local sites that already rank for the service.

The reviews still have to hold up after the AI picks you.
BrightLocal found 97% of people who use AI for local picks sometimes double-check the reviews.

Type "best plumber in" plus your town into ChatGPT today.
Write down every site it cites, then check whether you are on each one.

Source: Whitespark, 2025. BrightLocal Local Consumer Review Survey, 2026.

#LocalSEO #AIsearch

topic: Agency lock-in contracts / the one location setting that saves the most money in local Google Ads
caption:
A 12 month lock-in tells you how much an agency trusts its own results.

Search work takes months, so asking for a fair run is honest.
Google's guidance on hiring an SEO used to say four months to a year before you see the benefits.

The problem is a long term with no way out.

Before you sign anything, ask four things:
What is the notice period?
Who owns the Google Ads, Analytics and Search Console accounts?
Which number has to move, and by which month?
What happens if it does not?

Our SEO runs month to month with thirty days notice.
That keeps us honest, because leaving us is easy every single month.

If an agency will not name a point where you can walk away, believe it.

What is the longest marketing contract you have ever been stuck in?

Source: Google Search Central, "Do you need an SEO?", archived April 2026.

#SmallBusiness #SEO
alt: Tweet-style card from Mohd Farhan saying a 12 month contract does not keep a client, results do. If an agency needs a lock-in to keep you, it already knows the answer.

topic: Agency lock-in contracts / the one location setting that saves the most money in local Google Ads
caption:
The cheapest fix I know in a local Google Ads account takes one minute and sits under Location options.

The default setting is called "Presence or interest".
Google's help page says it shows your ads to people in your area and to people who have shown interest in it, wherever they are.

Google's own example is a bakery in Paris.
With the default, someone in Lyon reading about Paris can see the ad.

For an electrician in Dallas, that interest click costs the same as a local one.
It almost never turns into a job.

How to change it:
Open the campaign, then Settings, then Locations.
Expand Location options.
Pick "Presence: people in or regularly in your included locations".
Save, then check where your users were a week later.

I check this before I look at a single keyword in a new local account.
It is often the only change that needs no testing at all.

Have you ever checked where your ad clicks came from?

Source: Google Ads Help, advanced location options.

#GoogleAds #PPC

topic: 3 stages of DIY Facebook ads / 3 stages of a new Google Ads account
caption:
Boosting a post is the most expensive way to decide that Facebook ads "do not work".

A boosted post is built for engagement.
So Meta finds people who like and comment, not people who book a job.

That is why the likes climb and the phone stays quiet.

For leads, the campaign has to live in Ads Manager with the Leads objective.
Then the budget has to be big enough for Meta to learn.
Meta says an ad set usually leaves its learning phase after about 50 results in a week.

LocaliQ and WordStream put Home and Home Improvement leads on Facebook at $42.95 in 2026.
Fifty of those is about $2,150 a week for a single ad set.

A $50 boost was never going to get close.
So it cannot tell a cleaning company owner whether Meta works for them.

If you want a fair test, start with one ad set, one offer and an instant form in Ads Manager.
Then judge it on booked jobs.

What did your first boosted post teach you?

Source: Meta Business Help Center. LocaliQ and WordStream Facebook benchmarks, 2026.

#MetaAds #SmallBusiness

topic: 3 stages of DIY Facebook ads / 3 stages of a new Google Ads account
caption:
The quickest way to break a new Google Ads account is to change everything on day 9.

Google says a new bid strategy can show "Learning" for up to 7 days.
It says to judge results over 2 conversion cycles or 2 weeks, whichever is longer.

That is a long time for a dental clinic owner to watch money go out with only a few calls coming in.
So the temptation is to change bids, keywords and ads all at once.
A big edit can put the strategy back into learning, and the clock starts again.

What I do in the first 14 days instead:
Read the search terms every 2 or 3 days and add negatives.
Check that every conversion is a real call or a real form.
Leave bids and budget alone unless something is plainly broken.

Then judge it.
For Smart Bidding targets, Google wants at least 30 conversions in the period you read.

A new account looks worst in week one and is easiest to ruin in week two.

What did you change too early on your last campaign?

Source: Google Ads Help, bid strategy status and Smart Bidding.

#GoogleAds #PPC

topic: Why traffic does not become booked jobs (old reviews, slow replies, no prices) / junk keywords in an HVAC account
caption:
Three holes sit between a website visit and a booked job, and most ad money pours straight through them.

Hole one: old reviews.
BrightLocal's 2026 survey found 74% of consumers look for reviews from the last three months.
A 4.9 rating with nothing new since summer reads like a business that slowed down.

Hole two: slow replies.
Valve+Meter sent service requests to 466 US home services companies.
95% did not reply within five minutes, and 40% never replied in five days.

Hole three: no prices.
Nielsen Norman Group found buyers rank pricing as the information they most need online.
When it is missing, they leave for a competitor.
Even a starting price keeps them reading.

The owner of a 3-truck HVAC company can fix all three this month.
None of them needs a bigger ad budget.

Which of the three is your website leaking through right now?

Source: BrightLocal, 2026. Valve+Meter speed-to-lead test. Nielsen Norman Group.

#ConversionRate #SmallBusiness

topic: Why traffic does not become booked jobs (old reviews, slow replies, no prices) / junk keywords in an HVAC account
caption:
$188 of this example week went to people who were never going to book a furnace repair.

Job hunters, students, DIY fixers and someone shopping for a space heater.
None of them want a technician at the door.

The other $444 bought what the account is for.
Repair, emergency and installation searches from people with a cold house.

This adds up fast.
Our own worked example: a plumber spending $3,000 a month with 10% of clicks going to junk loses $3,600 a year.

How I clean it:
Open the Search terms report.
Sort by cost, highest first.
Add each junk word as a negative: jobs, course, how to, for sale.
Repeat it every week while the account is new, then every two weeks.

Use phrase or exact match negatives with care.
"Repair cost" is a buyer, but "repair course" is not.

Which junk word turns up most in your search terms?

topic: AI search: who uses ChatGPT by age / how little traffic AI tools send so far
caption:
61% of Americans aged 18 to 29 use ChatGPT, but only 19% of people 65 and over do.

That gap is the most useful AI number I have seen for a small business owner.

Pew Research Center asked US adults in February 2026.
44% of all adults said they use ChatGPT, up from 18% in 2023.
By age it was 61%, 55%, 37% and 19%, youngest to oldest.

So "are my customers using AI?" has a real answer, and it depends on who buys from you.
A med spa selling to people in their 20s and 30s is in a different world from a stair lift installer.

A lot of AI searching also happens inside Google, not in a separate app.
Alphabet said in July 2026 that AI Mode had passed 1 billion monthly users.
Your Google Business Profile and reviews still feed those answers.

Before you change your marketing for AI, write down the age range of your last 20 customers.

Source: Pew Research Center, 2026. Alphabet Q2 2026 earnings remarks.

#AIsearch #SmallBusiness

topic: AI search: who uses ChatGPT by age / how little traffic AI tools send so far
caption:
0.32% of website visits came from AI tools in early 2026, across more than 100,000 sites.

SE Ranking studied Google Analytics data from 101,574 sites, January to April 2026.
Organic search sent 42.75% of visits on the same sites, about 134 times more.
ChatGPT sent 74.78% of the AI share, and Gemini 11.56%.

The trend still matters.
The AI share was 0.02% in 2024 and 0.24% in 2025.

What I set up in GA4 so an owner can watch it:
A custom channel group called AI.
Referrals from chatgpt.com, gemini.google.com and perplexity.ai sorted into it.
A monthly look at enquiries from that channel, not visits.

One limit to know.
AI apps that pass no referrer show up as direct traffic, so the true share is a little higher than any study shows.

For a local plumber, that still means search and the map pack carry the phone this year.

What share of your visits came from AI tools last month?

Source: SE Ranking AI traffic study, 2026.

caption:
10.4K clicks from Google in six months, and for the first three of them the line barely moved.

This is a real Search Console screenshot from one client, August 2024 to February 2025.

9.2K clicks and 627K impressions in six months, from a site that sat flat until late November.

Search Console, 11 August 2024 to 7 February 2025.
Click rate 1.5%.

That last number looks bad, and I am leaving it in.

Clicks on searches that do not include the business name.
Which pages gained, from the Pages tab.
Any new errors in the Page indexing report.

The curve bent upward in late November and kept climbing into February.
Three flat months is normal for SEO, which is why I report clicks and enquiries from week one.

topic: The fortune is in the follow-up / the best keyword is the one your customer says out loud
caption:
85% of home services companies never made a second attempt to reach a new lead in one secret-shopper test.

Valve+Meter sent service requests to 466 US home services companies and timed the replies for five days.
The fastest answer came in 2 minutes.
85% did not try a second call.

Now put that next to how homeowners buy.
Modernize found 42.02% compare two quotes, 27.90% compare three and 15.64% compare four or more.

So the quote a roofer sends on Monday is sitting next to two others by Thursday.
The roofer who calls on Friday to answer questions is the one still in the conversation.

A follow-up schedule that works for most contractors:
Day 1, a short thank you with the quote attached again.
Day 3, a call to ask what questions came up.
Day 7, one photo of a similar finished job.
Day 14, a last check-in, then stop.

How many times does your business follow up on a quote before it lets it go?

Source: Valve+Meter speed-to-lead test. Modernize homeowner data.

#Sales #SmallBusiness

topic: The fortune is in the follow-up / the best keyword is the one your customer says out loud
caption:
Your customers rarely search the words printed on your price list.

A roofer calls it "roof replacement".
The homeowner types "roof leaking after rain" or "how much for a new roof".

Google says 15% of the searches it sees every day are new to it.
No keyword tool can list them all.

The best source I know is already in the account: the words people use on the phone.

What I do with a new account:
Listen to 10 recorded calls, or read the call notes.
Write down the exact phrases callers use for their problem.
Find those phrases in the search terms report and check what they cost.
Build one ad group around the phrase that brings the most calls.

Then write the headline in the same words, so the ad repeats what the person typed.

One caution before you record anything.
Consent rules differ by state, and California needs every party on the call to agree.

What phrase do your customers use that you would never have written yourself?

Source: Google, How Search Works.

#GoogleAds #PPC
alt: Quote card from Nasir Ahmad: The best keyword is the one your customer says out loud, not the one your tool suggests.

topic: Website redesign without redirects kills rankings / agency report full of impressions and no calls
caption:
A new website can wipe out years of Google rankings in a week when nobody redirects the old page addresses.

It usually goes like this.
The designer builds a lovely site.
The page that ranked for "water heater repair" used to live at one address.
Now it lives at another, and the old address shows an error.

Google finds a dead page, and the ranking that page earned goes with it.

Google's advice is plain.
Point every old URL to its new one with a permanent 301 redirect.
Keep those redirects for as long as possible, and at least a year.

The second trap is worse.
Many website builders have a setting that asks search engines not to index the site, and it gets left on at launch.
Google says once it reads that noindex rule, it drops the page from results entirely.

Before your designer launches, ask for one thing.
A spreadsheet of every old URL and the new page it now points to.

If they cannot make one, the launch can wait a week.

Has your web designer ever mentioned redirects to you?

Source: Google Search Central, site moves and noindex guidance.

#SEO #WebDesign
alt: Crayon comic: an owner loves his new website, then is shocked the calls stopped. A screen shows clicks steady before launch, a drop on launch day and old URLs returning 404 with no redirects.

topic: Website redesign without redirects kills rankings / agency report full of impressions and no calls
caption:
An impression counts every time your site appears in Google, even at position 80 on page eight.

That is how a monthly report can show impressions climbing while the phone stays quiet.

Search Console counts an impression when your result appears, whether or not anyone scrolled to it.
Backlinko's study of about 4 million Google results found 0.63% of searchers clicked anything on page two.

So a jump in impressions often means more rankings on pages nobody reads.

When I build a monthly report, the top row is enquiries:
Calls from Google that lasted over 60 seconds.
Form fills from real people, with spam removed.
Calls and direction requests from the Business Profile.

Non-brand clicks come next.
Impressions go near the bottom, as an early sign that a new topic is starting to show.

If your report opens with impressions, ask for it to be rebuilt around calls.

What is the first number on the report you got this month?

Source: Google Search Console Help. Backlinko CTR study.

#SEO #LocalSEO
alt: Crayon comic: an owner celebrates impressions going way up, then asks where the calls are. Notes show impressions way up, average position better and calls not shown.

topic: Break-up week: leaving an agency when it holds your logins / clients in love with vanity metrics
caption:
Leaving an agency should take one email, not three months of chasing logins.

With Valentine's Day less than three weeks away, break-ups are on my mind.
The messy ones start the same way: the agency owns the accounts.

Before you send that email, check four things:
You have admin access to your own Google Ads account.
You are a verified owner in Search Console.
You have admin rights on Google Analytics and your Google Business Profile.
You hold the logins for your website host and your domain.

Google's setup is why this matters.
In Search Console, owners can add and remove other users.
Whoever holds that role decides who stays.

If the agency holds all of it, ask for ownership to move to you first.
End the contract only after that.

An agency that trusts its own work hands everything over the same week.

Which of your accounts would be hardest to get back today?

Source: Google Search Console Help, owner permissions.

topic: Break-up week: leaving an agency when it holds your logins / clients in love with vanity metrics
caption:
A high click rate is the easiest number in an ad account to fall in love with, and on its own it pays nothing.

The vanity set looks like this:
Click rate going up.
Cost per click going down.
Impressions at a record high.

Each one can improve while the business books fewer jobs.
A cheap click from a job seeker is still a wasted click.

The numbers I want clients to love instead:
Cost per real lead, checked against the call log.
Leads that turned into booked jobs.
Revenue from those jobs, even a rough figure.

For a yardstick, LocaliQ's 2026 benchmarks put the average search lead at $90.92 for home and home improvement.
Compare your cost per lead to that, not to last month's click rate.

If the click rate rises and the call log stays empty, the ads are finding the wrong people faster.

Which metric did you fall for before you learned it did not pay?

Source: LocaliQ search advertising benchmarks, 2026.

#GoogleAds #PPC

topic: Things that need a sign to work: a pull door everyone pushes (Farhan, contact forms that confuse people into quitting) and unlabeled jars (Nasir, leads with no source label)
caption:
If a door needs a sign that says PULL, the door is badly built.

Website contact forms have the same problem, and it costs enquiries every day.

Zuko tracked 739 forms from January 2022 to April 2025.
Only 51.7% of people who started a form finished it.
Of everyone who saw one, 34.6% completed it.

Zuko found little link between form length and conversion.
Relevance and clarity mattered more than the number of fields.

What confuses people on a plumber's or a dentist's form:
↳ Grey hint text inside the box instead of a label above it.
Nielsen Norman Group testing found this hurts usability, because the hint vanishes once you type.
↳ No sign of which fields are required.
Baymard found only 14% of desktop sites and 6% of mobile sites mark both required and optional fields.
↳ A button that says "Submit" when it could say "Get my quote".

Each one is a small PULL sign taped to the door.

Fill in your own form on your phone tonight, and notice the moment you are unsure what to do next.

Sources: Zuko, 2025. Nielsen Norman Group. Baymard Institute.

#WebDesign #ConversionRate

topic: Things that need a sign to work: a pull door everyone pushes (Farhan, contact forms that confuse people into quitting) and unlabeled jars (Nasir, leads with no source label)
caption:
A shelf of identical jars with no labels is how a lot of lead lists look from the inside.

A name, a phone number, a date.
Nothing that says where the person came from.

Then the owner of a 3-van plumbing company asks the monthly question: which channel gets more money?
Each platform answers it with its own rules.
Google Ads, Meta and GA4 count conversions their own way, so their totals add up to more customers than the business has.

Google Ads now offers two attribution models, last click and data-driven.
Neither sees a neighbor's tip, a review site or a ChatGPT answer.
BrightLocal's 2026 survey found 45% of consumers now use AI tools for local recommendations.

What I set up so every lead carries a label:
1. One sheet, one row per customer, with the source and the value of the first job.
2. The source filled in from the ad click wherever tracking can see it.
3. One question on every call and form: "How did you hear about us?"
4. A monthly look at that sheet next to what each platform claims.

That sheet is the number you report to yourself.
The platforms are for comparing ads with each other.

Sources: Google Ads Help. BrightLocal Local Consumer Review Survey, 2026.

#MarketingAttribution #GoogleAds

topic: Prices up front as a filter: Farhan on why Mavix shows starting prices on its site, Nasir on putting a starting price in the Google Ads headline so the wrong people never click
caption:
Every plan on our website has shown a starting price since October 2026.

The usual agency advice is to hide the number until the sales call.
We think that wastes the owner's time first and ours second.

The owner of a 3-truck HVAC company wants one answer before anything else: can I afford these people?
If he has to book a call to find out, plenty of owners close the tab instead.

The research points the same way.
BrightLocal's 2019 survey of local business websites listed missing prices and out-of-date prices among the errors that put people off.
Baymard found 40% of US shoppers who abandoned a checkout did it over extra costs they had not expected.

Surprise costs are what drive people away.

A starting price will cost us some enquiries.
Mostly the ones that would have ended in "too expensive" after the proposal.

What our pages show:
↳ SEO from $1,000 a month, with no setup fee.
↳ Paid ads from $35 per qualified lead, with no monthly fee.
↳ Month to month, with 30 days notice.

The exact price still comes after a free review, in writing.

Sources: BrightLocal, 2019. Baymard Institute.

Does your website show any price at all today?

#SmallBusiness #Pricing

topic: Prices up front as a filter: Farhan on why Mavix shows starting prices on its site, Nasir on putting a starting price in the Google Ads headline so the wrong people never click
caption:
A starting price in the ad itself is the cheapest filter I know in Google Ads, because the people it puts off never cost you a click.

You pay when someone clicks, not when they buy.
Every bargain hunter who taps the ad, sees the price on the page and leaves is money spent on the wrong person.

LocaliQ's 2025 benchmarks put the median home services click at $7.85, and up to $13.74 for painting.

A headline like "Drain cleaning from $189" (an example price) moves that filter in front of the click.

How I test it:
1. Responsive search ads take up to 15 headlines of 30 characters, so one of them can carry the price.
2. Run it as a second ad in the same ad group, since Google suggests at least 2 per ad group anyway.
3. Judge it on cost per booked job, and expect the click rate to fall, because that is the filter doing its job.

It does not suit every business.
A price puts off people hunting for the cheapest job, which helps a premium roofer and can hurt a budget cleaner.

If price is your weak point, use that headline for something else you win on.

Sources: LocaliQ Home Services Benchmarks, 2025. Google Ads Help.

#GoogleAds #PPC

topic: Page speed on phones: how few mobile sites pass Google's speed checks (Farhan, HTTP Archive) and what 0.1 seconds did to lead form visits in the Deloitte study, seen from inside ad accounts (Nasir)
caption:
Fewer than half of mobile websites pass all three of Google's page speed checks.

The HTTP Archive's 2025 Web Almanac, using July 2025 data, put it at 48%.
The weakest check was the main content loading in time.
Only 62% of mobile sites passed that one.

For an owner, that is the check to care about.
It measures how long a visitor stares at a blank or half-built page.
Google's target is 2.5 seconds or less.

On a small business site the cause is usually on a short list:
↳ A huge photo at the top of the page.
↳ Slow, cheap hosting.
↳ Plugins, sliders and chat widgets nobody uses.

One warning before you pay anyone for speed work.
Google says it still shows the most relevant page even when the page experience is poor.
Speed will not rescue a page that does not answer the search.
It decides what happens after the visitor arrives.

Test it yourself on your phone, on mobile data, away from the office Wi-Fi.
If your homepage takes longer than about 3 seconds to show its main content, start there.

Sources: HTTP Archive Web Almanac, 2025. Google Search Central.

#PageSpeed #SmallBusiness
alt: Horizontal bar chart from the HTTP Archive Web Almanac 2025: 62 percent of mobile sites pass the main content load check, 77 percent the tap response check, 81 percent the layout stability check and 48 percent pass all three.

topic: Page speed on phones: how few mobile sites pass Google's speed checks (Farhan, HTTP Archive) and what 0.1 seconds did to lead form visits in the Deloitte study, seen from inside ad accounts (Nasir)
caption:
In a Google-commissioned Deloitte study, a mobile site 0.1 seconds faster came with 21.6% more lead generation visitors reaching the form page.

The study covered 37 brand sites and over 30 million sessions in late 2019.
Big brands, and Google paid for it, so treat it as direction.

The mechanism is what I see in ad accounts.
You pay for the click the moment it happens.
If a dentist's landing page is still loading 4 seconds later, the visitor goes back to the results and taps the next ad.
The click stays on your bill.

What I check before raising a bid on a lead campaign:
1. Run the landing page through PageSpeed Insights on mobile.
2. Read the real-user section at the top first, since the score below it is only a lab test.
3. Check the main content loads in 2.5 seconds or less, which is Google's good threshold.
4. Make sure the top image is not lazy-loaded, which Google's own guide says never to do.

A faster landing page rarely needs a new website.
Most of the time it needs a smaller photo and fewer scripts.

Sources: Deloitte for Google, Milliseconds Make Millions. Google web.dev.

#GoogleAds #PageSpeed
alt: Dark stat card showing 21.6 percent more visitors reached the lead form when a mobile site loaded 0.1 seconds faster, with a tile noting Google's 2.5 second good score for main content load time.

topic: Impatience with the wrong number: an owner checking SEO rankings every day (Farhan) and Meta instant form leads that are cheap until you call them (Nasir)
caption:
Checking your Google rankings every morning is the quickest way to quit SEO a few weeks before it starts paying.

Rankings shift by the day and by the searcher.
The position you see from your office is one view out of many.

Google's own guidance says a change can take from a few hours to several months to show, and suggests waiting a few weeks before judging it.
Getting a page crawled again can take days or weeks after you ask.

Our working estimate is three to six months before commercial searches move, and about a year in a crowded category.

The owner of a roofing company does not need a daily rank check.
He needs to know the right numbers are moving, in the right order:
1. Pages indexed.
2. Impressions on searches without your business name.
3. Clicks on those searches.
4. Calls and forms.

If the first two are rising in month two, the last two are usually on the way.
If nothing on that list has moved by month four, ask your agency hard questions.

Source: Google Search Central documentation.

Which number do you look at first when your SEO report arrives?

#SEO #LocalSEO

topic: Impatience with the wrong number: an owner checking SEO rankings every day (Farhan) and Meta instant form leads that are cheap until you call them (Nasir)
caption:
Meta instant forms make leads cheap for one reason: the form opens inside Facebook with the person's name, email and phone already filled in.

That is also why some people forget they ever sent it.

A cheap lead price tells you nothing about how many of those people answer the phone.
Meta knows this too.
Since April 2026, new campaigns can only use its qualified leads goal if a CRM is connected through the Conversions API.

What I change on a lead form campaign for a local service business:
1. Switch the form type to higher intent, which adds a review screen before it sends.
2. Add one question only a real buyer can answer, like the job and the zip code.
3. Call or text within minutes, while they still remember tapping it.
4. Download leads every day or connect a CRM, because Meta keeps instant form leads available for only 90 days.

Then judge the campaign on cost per booked job.
A form at half the lead price only wins if it books more than half as well as your landing page.

Source: Meta Business Help Center.

#MetaAds #LeadGeneration

topic: Receipts read past the headline number: $178.6K of Meta spend for one online store judged campaign by campaign (Farhan) and 101K Search Console impressions where 98 in 100 people scrolled past (Nasir)
caption:
$178,644.90 spent on Meta Ads for one online store between July 2022 and August 2025.

141,456 link clicks, which works out at about $1.26 a click across three years.
The top campaigns returned between 2.00 and 6.05 in purchase ROAS.

The range matters more than the total.

A 6.05 campaign brings back about $6 in sales for every $1 of spend.
A 2.00 campaign brings back $2, and once product, shipping and fees are paid, that can leave almost nothing.

So an owner who only reads the blended number can be paying for a weak campaign out of a strong one's profit, and never notice.

The habit that matters on an account this size is a dull one.
Read each campaign on its own, against the store's real margin, before moving a dollar of budget.

The report is real.
The client name stays private.

DM me "META" and I will show you how we read a report like this one.

topic: Receipts read past the headline number: $178.6K of Meta spend for one online store judged campaign by campaign (Farhan) and 101K Search Console impressions where 98 in 100 people scrolled past (Nasir)
caption:
Google showed this site 101K times in six months, and about 98 times in every 100 nobody clicked.

Search Console, one client, 27 June to late December 2024.
1.81K clicks from 101K impressions.
CTR 1.8%, at an average position of 30.9.

Clicks started climbing in October.
The number I keep coming back to is the 1.8%.

At an average position near 31, a low click rate is expected.
Still, every impression is a search where Google already put you on the page.
The title is the one line a searcher reads before deciding.

What the research says about titles:
↳ Zyppy studied 80,959 titles across 2,370 sites and found Google rewrote 61.6% of them.
↳ Rewrites were least common for titles of 51 to 60 characters.

For a service page, the shape I use is the service, the place, one reason to choose you, then the brand.

Then measure it properly.
Compare CTR in Search Console for four weeks before and after, at a similar average position.

Screenshot from Google Search Console, June to December 2024. Title data: Zyppy.

DM me "titles" and I will check the page titles on your top pages.

topic: What clean data looks like: a week of leads where every one is traced to its source (Farhan, stack) and a week of Meta spend split by placement with the junk ones struck out (Nasir, list)
caption:
This is what a normal week of leads looks like once tracking works, and many owners have never seen one.

Each call, form and booking sits next to the time it came in and the channel that sent it.
The video shows an example week with made-up numbers.

Without tracking, the same week sounds like this: "The phone was busy, so I think the ads are working."

With it, you can answer the one question that matters on a Friday afternoon.
Where should next month's money go?

The setup is the least exciting part of marketing, and everything after it depends on it:
1. Google Analytics 4, Search Console, Tag Manager and Google Ads, linked to each other.
2. A written rule for what counts as an enquiry.
3. Call tracking, so phone leads stop being invisible.
4. One test call and one test form, checked in every system.
5. The lead source saved on the contact, because GA4 looks back 90 days at most.

Then once a month, count the enquiries in your inbox and CRM and put them beside what the platforms report.
If the numbers drift apart, something broke.

Source: Google Analytics Help.

If you could see last week like this, what would you stop paying for?

#MarketingAttribution #SmallBusiness

topic: What clean data looks like: a week of leads where every one is traced to its source (Farhan, stack) and a week of Meta spend split by placement with the junk ones struck out (Nasir, list)
caption:
In this example, $132 of a $490 week went to placements that never sent a lead worth calling.

The numbers are made up.
The shape is one I keep finding in Meta accounts for local trades like cleaners and roofers.

Advantage+ placements spread the budget across Facebook, Instagram, Messenger and Audience Network.
Meta's delivery chases the cheapest results, and some placements are good at cheap results that never answer the phone.

How I find them:
1. In Ads Manager, break the report down by placement.
2. Put cost per lead next to how many of those leads booked a job.
3. Wait two weeks before judging, so one odd day does not decide it.
4. Turn off the placements whose leads never pick up, and leave the rest alone.

Audience Network is where I look first.
Those ads run inside other apps and games, where an accidental tap is easy and buying intent is low.

Do not exclude by habit, though.
On some accounts Reels or Stories bring the cheapest booked jobs, and cutting them would raise your costs.

topic: Trust you can measure: long-term clients come from one small promise kept on a date both sides can see (Farhan), and ad arguments end when you split test them (Nasir)
caption:
The clients who stay for years are rarely the ones we promised the most.

They are the ones we promised one clear thing, and then hit it.

That is why our SEO guarantee is small on purpose.
On the Growth and Scale plans, it is a 50% rise in organic traffic, keyword rankings or direct enquiries within 90 days.
Miss it, and the client gets every retainer fee back plus $1,000.

We could write a bigger promise.
Page one for every service in every town, inside a year.
It would win more first meetings and lose more clients by month six.

A small promise builds trust in a few plain ways:
↳ The baseline is measured in the client's own Search Console and GA4 in week one, so nobody argues about the starting point.
↳ Day 90 is a date both sides can see coming.
↳ Once we hit it, the next goal gets set from real numbers.

Bigger goals still exist.
They sit in the plan as month six aims, and we call them aims.

If an agency has ever promised you the moon, what did month four look like?

#SEO #SmallBusiness

topic: Trust you can measure: long-term clients come from one small promise kept on a date both sides can see (Farhan), and ad arguments end when you split test them (Nasir)
caption:
The loudest opinion in a meeting about ads is usually the least tested one, and that includes mine.

A typical example.
The client is sure the headline needs his 25 years in business.
I am sure it needs the price.
Neither of us knows.

Google Ads has a tool for exactly this.
Custom experiments split a campaign's traffic and budget evenly between the original and a trial copy.
One person sees one version, so the comparison is fair.

How I run one on a small account:
1. Change one thing only, such as the headline, the landing page or the bid strategy.
2. Pick the measure before it starts, and make it cost per qualified lead.
3. Leave it running 4 to 6 weeks, which is what Google's experiments guidance recommends.
4. Do not stop early because week one looks good.

Whoever turns out to be wrong, the account wins.
The next argument starts from a number.

One limit: a tiny account may not have enough traffic for a fair split.
Then I test big changes only, and listen to the calls.

Source: Google Ads Help, custom experiments.

What would you test first if the traffic were split for you?

#GoogleAds #PPC

topic: Sending people to the wrong place: an owner who asks for more traffic when he wants more customers (Farhan) and a water heater ad that lands on the homepage (Nasir)
caption:
An owner who asks for more traffic usually wants more customers, and those are two different jobs.

Traffic is easy to get.
A blog post on fixing a dripping tap can pull thousands of visits to a plumber's site.
Almost none of those readers will ever book a plumber.

So before anyone promises more visitors, we check three things:
1. Where the visits land: service pages, or articles for people doing it themselves?
2. Where the visitors are: inside your service area, or three states away?
3. Whether leads are counted at all, because taps on a mobile call button often go untracked.

Then we split the clicks properly.
Since March 2026, Search Console's branded queries filter has been open to all eligible sites.
It separates searches for your name from searches for what you do.
People who typed your name would have found you anyway, so the non-brand clicks are the ones SEO earned.

Your Google Business Profile counts as well.
Calls, direction requests and website clicks from the map are customers, even when they never show up as website traffic.

Source: Google Search Central, 2026.

Would you rather have 1,000 more visits next month, or 10 more calls?

#SEO #SmallBusiness

topic: Sending people to the wrong place: an owner who asks for more traffic when he wants more customers (Farhan) and a water heater ad that lands on the homepage (Nasir)
caption:
An ad for water heater repair that lands on the homepage makes the visitor search twice.

They tapped an ad about one job.
They land on a page about twelve.
The phone number is there somewhere, but the water heater is not.

Google notices this too.
Landing page experience is one of the three parts of Quality Score, next to expected click-through rate and ad relevance.
Google also lists the quality of your ads and landing page among the factors behind Ad Rank.

What I check in every Search campaign:
↳ Each ad group's final URL matches its keywords.
↳ The page names the job in the first headline.
↳ A price range and the phone number sit above the fold.

The homepage can be fine for a business with a single service, or for searches of your own business name.

If you are unsure, send one ad group to a page built for that job for a month, and compare cost per lead.

One thing to know: there is no good public study comparing homepage and landing page for the same ads.
Treat any precise uplift figure you are quoted with suspicion.

Source: Google Ads Help, Quality Score and Ad Rank.

Which ad group in your account still points at the homepage?

#GoogleAds #LandingPages

topic: Three months in, the honest checklist: the sourcing rule that shaped every post (Farhan) and the Networks box Nasir checks in nearly every Google Ads account he audits (Nasir)
caption:
Three months and 38 posts in, the rule that cost us the most time was this one: no number goes up without a source we can name.

Every figure here had to come from a named study, an official help page or a screenshot from an account we run, or be clearly marked as an example.

That rule killed some good-looking posts.
"62% of calls to small businesses go unanswered" is quoted everywhere.
We went looking for the original report and could not find it, so it never appeared here.
We used Invoca's 2026 measured figure instead: 52% of calls to home services firms reached a person.

Two more things these three months taught us.

Writing for owners is harder than writing for marketers.
An owner skips any line he cannot use the same day, so every post had to carry one thing to do.

Nasir and I write every idea twice, in our own words.
It doubles the work.
It is also why his feed and mine do not read like copies of each other.

Which marketing stat have you seen quoted so often that nobody checks it anymore?

#Marketing #SmallBusiness

topic: Three months in, the honest checklist: the sourcing rule that shaped every post (Farhan) and the Networks box Nasir checks in nearly every Google Ads account he audits (Nasir)
caption:
Every new Google Ads Search campaign starts with search partners switched on, and most owners never open that setting.

Search partners are sites and apps outside Google, including YouTube search results, where your Search ads can also show.
Google's own help page says those clicks "may not always reflect highly targeted traffic".

For a plumber paying for every click, that line is worth reading twice.
Still, partners are not always bad.
Opteo looked at about 10,000 accounts and found search partner conversions cost a median 7% more than Google Search ones.
Some accounts did far better on partners, and some far worse.

So I never switch them off by habit.
What I check:
1. Segment the campaign by network.
2. Compare cost per lead on Google Search against search partners.
3. If partners spent money with no leads, untick them under Networks in the campaign settings.
4. Add the {network} tracking parameter so every lead records where it came from.

One more thing for February.
Google says Search campaigns with Display turned on move to channel prioritization from this month, and spend between channels may shift.
That box sits right next to this one, so check both while you are there.

Sources: Google Ads Help. Opteo, about 10,000 accounts.

#GoogleAds #PPC

topic: Big budgets vs real ones: copying a big game TV splash on a local budget (Farhan) and a client who asks for a 10x ROAS target (Nasir)
caption:
Big brands paid millions of dollars for 30 seconds of TV this month, and they can afford to wait a long time for it to pay off.

A local roofer cannot.
He needs the phone to ring this week.

The small business answer to a big game budget is a boring one.
A modest amount, spent every day, on people already searching for the job.

What $1,000 a month buys on Google Ads, on average:
↳ $32.89 a day, because Google counts a month as 30.4 days.
↳ About 185 clicks at LocaliQ's 2026 all-industry average of $5.42 a click.
↳ About 15 leads at the $66.69 average cost per lead.

In home improvement, where a lead averaged $90.92, the same $1,000 buys about 11.

Eleven leads will never make a highlight reel.
They can be traced to booked jobs, which one big splash on local TV almost never can.

Copy the brands on one thing only: they show up where their buyers already are.
For a roofer, that is a search for "roof leak repair" at 7 AM.

Source: LocaliQ Search Advertising Benchmarks, 2026. Google Ads Help.

How much of your budget reaches people who are already looking?

#GoogleAds #SmallBusiness

topic: Big budgets vs real ones: copying a big game TV splash on a local budget (Farhan) and a client who asks for a 10x ROAS target (Nasir)
caption:
A 10x ROAS target on a small Shopify store's account usually means the ads stop showing, and then the ads get the blame.

Google warns about this on its own help page.
It says a target set too high may limit the traffic your ads get.
The bidding only enters auctions where it expects that return, and there are few of them.

Before I set any ROAS target, I work out two things with the client.

First, the break-even.
Break-even ROAS is 1 divided by your margin.
A 37.5% margin breaks even at 2.67.
NYU Stern's January 2026 data puts apparel gross margins at 56.88%, which breaks even at 1.76.

Second, ratio or profit.
8x on $1,000 of spend is $8,000 in sales.
4x on $5,000 of spend is $20,000 in sales.
At a 50% margin, the first leaves $3,000 after ad cost and the second leaves $5,000.

Target ROAS also needs 15 conversions in the last 30 days on Search and Shopping, per Google.
Below that, a tight target has little to learn from.

So I start near the ROAS the campaign already hits, then raise it in small steps once results hold.

Source: Google Ads Help, target ROAS. NYU Stern margin data, January 2026.

#GoogleAds #ROAS
alt: Dark tweet-style card where a client asks for a 10x ROAS and the target goes in at 1,000 percent, followed by a reaction GIF of a tumbleweed rolling past.
